en: The Khādira Gṛhyasūtra and the Drāhyāyaṇa Gṛhyasūtra: Now, therefore, the domestic rites. 1. When no specific time is prescribed, the proper time for [the performance of] rites is during the northern course of the sun, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day, before the turning of the sun [at midday]. 2.
At the conclusion, he should feed as many Brāhmaṇas as he can afford;
[he should wear] the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) [made of] wool (sautra).
Having fastened the hem of his garment around his neck, he raises his right arm and becomes one who wears the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī);
having placed it over the left [arm], he becomes one who wears it over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).
Having sipped water three times, he should wipe his mouth twice;
having sprinkled his feet, he should sprinkle his head;
and he should touch the sense organs with water.
Finally, having sipped water for purification, he becomes pure.
(12) His sitting, standing, and reclining shall be upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing north. (13) He should receive [the instruction] while facing east. (14)
15. Behind the fire is where the oblation (homa) should take place.
16. [The ritual] is performed together with the head at the sound of the bath. 17. When no specific instruction is given, the action is to be done with the right hand.
One should know that a mantra whose end is unmanifest is characterized by the inclusion of the beginning of the next [mantra] (18).
Mantras ending in *svāhā* are for burnt offerings (*homa*) (19).
That which is performed in a single fire is called a *pākayajña* (20).
Therein, the officiating priest (ṛtvij) acts as the Brahman; except for the morning and evening oblations (21), he himself performs the duties of the Hotṛ (22).
To the south of the fire, facing north, the Brahman sits silently until the oblation is offered on the eastward-pointed grass (23).
If he should utter a word concerning sacrifice, that is permissible; or, having uttered something unsuitable for sacrifice, he should mutter the Mahāvyāhṛtis (25),
or [the verse] "This [is] Viṣṇu" (26).

If he himself performs the duties of the *hautra* and *brahmatva*, having sat upon the seat of the *brahman* priest and placed there his umbrella, upper garment, or water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), he may then perform the other rites.
(27) He should desire that there be no turning away from the sacrifice and no interruption by the sacrificial limbs.
(28) Thus ends the first section.
Having smeared the eastern part of the house with cow-dung, one should make a mark in its center:
(1) having drawn a line from south to north,
(2) from its beginning toward the north, and from its end toward the east, (3) three lines toward the east in the middle.
Having sprinkled that [water] four times, having kindled the fire five times, and having swept around it with the three-verse hymn beginning with "imaṃ stomam" six times.

Afterwards, having placed his hands face down on the ground behind the fire, he recites "idaṃ bhūme" (this [is] the earth) ending with the word *vasu* at night. Having spread darbha grass behind [the fire], he should draw it out toward the east from the south and from the north.

Or, without drawing out the previous [grass], he should spread the grass around the fire from left to right, covering the roots with the tips, either in three layers or five layers. Having sat down, he cuts off two darbha tips, each a span long, not with his fingernail, saying: "You two are purifiers belonging to Viṣṇu."
Having wiped [the ladle] with water, [he says], "You two are purified by the mind of Viṣṇu. 13.

Grasping [the two strainers] with the thumbs and the two ring fingers, their tips pointing northward, he purifies the clarified butter three times, [saying]: "May the god Savitṛ purify you with a flawless strainer, with the rays of the sun, the Vasu.
14. Having sprinkled these two [strainers] with water, he should throw them into the fire. 15.

Having placed the clarified butter on the fire, he should perform [the following] to the north (verse 16). Bending his right knee, with his right hand, he should pour out a handful of water to the south of the fire, saying: "O Aditi, give your consent" (verse 17). To the west, saying: "O Anumati, give your consent" (verse 17); and to the north, saying: "O Sarasvatī, give your consent" (verse 18).
Saying, "O God Savitṛ, impel [the sacrifice]," he should sprinkle water around the fire from left to right while carrying the oblation around it—
either once or thrice— and having placed a fuel-stick upon the fire.

Having recited the *prapada* and become exhausted, one should meditate on what is auspicious and exhale while beginning with the *vairūpākṣa* [mantra]. (22) In rites for specific desires, this should be done according to each desire.
(23) One should perform this in all these burnt offerings (*homa*). (24)
Thus ends the second section:
Having studied the Veda and presented it to his teacher, the religious student (brahmacārī), being permitted by the teacher, shall take a wife; and he shall perform the ritual bath (āplavana).
Of these two, the ceremonial bath (āplavana) is performed first;
however, the seizing of the hand (pāṇigrahaṇa), preceded by the salutation with mantras, has already been explained.
A Brāhmaṇa, carrying a water-pot, covered, and maintaining silence, shall go before the fire and stand facing north.

Having bathed and clothed her in an unwashed garment, while she is being brought forward with the verses beginning "Those who cut [the wool]," the one who takes her hand should mutter the verse, "Soma gave her.
He should cause her to sit down to the south of the one who takes her hand.
While she holds on to him, he should offer clarified butter with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*) using the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), making oblations as they are performed.
The fourth [offering] is made with all [the verses] together;
likewise at the tonsure, the initiation, and the godāna ceremonies.
At the taking of the hand in marriage, [it is offered] with the six verses beginning with "May Agni come first."
There are no two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga) and no offering to Sviṣṭakṛt when there is no specific injunction regarding oblations of clarified butter.
In all cases, one should subsequently offer with the Mahāvyāhṛtis and with the verse dedicated to Prajāpati.
One should offer the expiatory oblations;
having offered them, the two rise up (Sūtra 15). Having gone behind [the fire] and standing to the south, he should take the joined palms of the bride (Sūtra 17).

The mother, having placed fried grains mixed with *śamī* leaves in a winnowing basket, shall cause the bride—who stands behind the fire—to step upon a stone with her right forefoot, [saying]: "Upon this stone...
(18-19). The brother shall pour the handful of fried grains, taken all at once, into the bride's joined palms (20).

Or some friend should offer him [the grain] into the fire without breaking the *añjali* gesture, with the mantra "This woman... (RV X.85.21). For the two following oblations, he should use the mantras "To Aryaman... (RV X.85.22) and "To Pūṣan... (RV X.85.23).
Having offered the oblation with that same [ladle], he should go around the fire keeping it to his right and lead the girl away from her paternal kin;
starting from the point of settling down, this is done three times.
Having poured the remainder from the winnowing basket into the fire, he should make her step forward toward the north-eastern direction with the words, "One for food."

The bridegroom’s inspection, the mounting of the chariot, and the consecration by Durgā should be performed with beautiful women. Having gone to the west of the fire, the priest of the water-element (Audaka) should pour water on the head of the bridegroom and on the bride.
"May they anoint [thee]"—thus he is sprinkled.
(30) He should take the right hand, including the thumb, with the six verses beginning "I take thy hand.
(31) Thus ends the third section.
He should lead her toward the north-eastern direction.

Having established the fire in the house of a Brāhmaṇa, he should spread out a red bull-hide behind the fire with the hair side up and the neck facing east; he should then cause her, while maintaining silence, to sit down upon it.

When the auspicious constellation has been announced, while she maintains contact with him, he should offer oblations with the dipping-spoon (sruva), pouring the remnants over the head of the bride during each of the six oblations beginning with the "line" (lekhā).
Having circumambulated the fire from left to right, he shows him the polar star (dhruva), saying, "Firm is the sky.
Having saluted his elders by their lineage name, he may release his speech.
A cow is the sacrificial fee.
Here, the *arghya* [is offered];
some say [it is offered] when [the guests] have arrived.
For three nights, avoiding pungent salt and milk, they two should lie down together while practicing celibacy (*brahmacārin*).
Having recited over the sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) the mantra "With the food-noose," he should utter the name of the bride, saying, "O so-and-so.
(10) Having eaten, he should give the remains to the bride.

(11) After three nights have passed, he should offer clarified butter (*ājya*) with four verses beginning with "O Agni, thou art atonement" (*agne prāyaścittiḥ*). He should pour the remnants of all five oblations into a water-pot. (12)
Therefore, he should bathe her along with her hair and nails;
then it will be according to the truth.
During the period favorable for conception, when she has completed her menstrual flow, he should touch her private parts with his right hand, saying: "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb. 13–15.
"May there be conception; take up the embryo"—this is the fourth section.
That fire in which one should take the hand is the *gṛhya* (domestic) fire.
Or, he may place the final fuel-stick on that fire; or it may be the fire produced by friction, for that is auspicious but not conducive to prosperity; or he may bring it from a frying pan.
Or [the fire] may be taken from the house of one who has performed many sacrifices, excluding a Śūdra;
the service begins with the evening oblation,
having kindled the fire before sunset and sunrise.

The oblation is performed when the sun has set (8), or when it has risen, or even before it has risen (9). If the sacrificial food has not been prepared, one should wash it and offer it with the hand (10).
If it is curd or milk, [he offers] with a bronze vessel or a cooking pot for the *caru* in the center, saying: "To Agni, svāhā! (11–13).
Silently, he offers the northern oblation toward the north-east.
(14) "To Sūrya," he says in the morning for the eastern oblation.
(15) In this case, the rites beginning with the sweeping around are omitted, with the exception of the sprinkling around. (16)
"According to some, the wife should offer the oblation (17).
'The house is the wife; this is the domestic fire' (18).
When it has been said, 'It is ready for the evening and morning [offerings],' she should say aloud, 'Om'" (19).

With the mantra "mākṣā namaste," he should offer oblations of sacrificial food (haviṣya) in a low voice (upāṃśu); he should offer the portion for Prajāpati and the Sviṣṭakṛt portion. He should then carry forth the bali offerings.
Having placed [the water] fourfold, either outside or inside, at the location of the jar (maṇika) or in the middle.
At the door (26), near the bed (27), or near the latrine (28).
Then, [he should perform] the *sastūpa* rite; he should sprinkle water around each [fire] on both sides;
he should pour out the remainder together with water toward the south.
When the husks have been offered with the formula, "Of the husks, [the portion] for Apāmārga," 32.
Earth, Vāyu, Prajāpati, the Viśvedevas, the Waters, the Plants and Trees, Ākāśa, Kāma, Manyu, the hosts of Rākṣasas, the Pitṛs, and Rudra are the deities of the *bali* offerings. 33.
However, one may perform these silently. 34.
35. One should perform this for all the food [prepared].
36. If [the food] is prepared at one time, one should perform it only once. 37. If there are many [portions], one should perform it for that which belongs to the householder.
Having offered the first portion of every kind of food into the fire and having given [a portion] to a Brāhmaṇa, he should eat himself.
From rice onwards until barley, or from barley onwards until rice, he should take [the portions] himself; he should take them himself.
Thus ends the fifth section.
Thus ends the first chapter: The New- and Full-Moon Sacrifices, beginning with the Full Moon. 1.
If the New-Moon sacrifice should present itself first, one should perform the Full-Moon sacrifice and then perform that [New-Moon sacrifice]. 2.
Some say that one who does not perform the Full Moon sacrifice should wait [for the next one]. 3.

Having bathed in the afternoon, the husband and wife should eat the *aupavasathika* (fast-day) meal. 4. Mānatantavya said: "He obtains excellent offspring and becomes desirable; he who eats the *aupavasathika* meal becomes gluttonous. 5.
Therefore, one should eat whatever one desires;
one should not practice what is contrary to the vow. Having offered the morning oblation—
One should pour out [the grain] with the formula, "I pour thee out, acceptable to such-and-such [deity]," once for the deity with the *yajus* formula, or twice silently;
one should wash it three times for the gods and twice for men.
Once, for the ancestors,
he should cook [the rice] with the stirring-spoon, turning it clockwise while lifting it up;
having poured clarified butter over the cooked rice, removed it from the fire toward the north, he should pour clarified butter over it once again.

Having thus placed all the sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi) upon the sacrificial grass (barhis), he should offer the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāgau). Having taken four spoonfuls of clarified butter, he should make them fivefold for the Bhṛgus who are descendants of Jamadagni; he offers with "Svāhā to Agni" on the north side, and with "To Soma" on the south side.

The others are the reverse. 18. Having spread a base of clarified butter (*ājya*), one should take a portion of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) with the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) from the middle and from the front; 19. and also from the back, if one is a performer of the five-fold division (*pañcāvattin*). 20.
Having sprinkled [the clarified butter] over it, he anoints the places from which the portions were cut;
this does not apply to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
He should offer it with the formula "Svāhā to such-and-such," according to whichever deity the offering belongs to.

Having spread an under-layer of ghee once for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering—twice for the Bhṛgus—and having poured ghee over the oblation twice, he should sacrifice in the north-eastern direction with the mantra: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, Svāhā! (24). Having placed a fuel-stick on the fire (25), and having thrice dipped blades of *darbha* grass into the clarified butter or the oblation—representing the tip, the middle, and the base—he sprinkles them while reciting: "Licking the offered [portion], may they depart as birds" (*aktaṃ rihāṇā viyantu vayaḥ*). Then he should cast them into the fire with the mantra: "O Rudra, lord of cattle, who moves along the ropes, the bull; do not harm our cattle. Let this be an offering for you, Svāhā! (26).
One should perform that sacrificial site-rite everywhere (27–28).
Having set aside the remnants of the oblation toward the north, one should give them to the Brahman priest (29).
A full vessel is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
or according to one's enthusiasm;
thus ends the first section.
1. For one who has not established the sacred fires, there is a sthālīpāka dedicated to Agni at the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
2. For one who has established the sacred fires, there is a sthālīpāka dedicated to Agni and Soma on the full moon day.
3. On the new moon day, it is dedicated to Indra, or to Mahendra, or to Indra and Agni.
Or, as in the case of one who has not established the sacred fires:
the entire day is the place for the morning oblation,
and the night is the place for the evening oblation.
The entire dark fortnight belongs to the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice; the bright fortnight belongs to the Dārśa sacrifice.
Some say that one should maintain the continuity by fasting.
If sacrificial offerings are unavailable, one should offer the fruits of sacrificial trees, or *palāśa* leaves, or water. 10–12.
For that which has been offered is indeed an expiation for that which has not been offered; one should offer clarified butter (ājya) when no specific oblation is prescribed.
The deities [are invoked] when the mantras have not been previously taught. In the third month of the first pregnancy, the *puṃsavana* (rite for ensuring a male child) is performed.
After she has bathed and is clothed in an unwashed garment, the husband, having offered oblations, should stand behind her.
Having touched the right shoulder, he should touch the uncovered region of the navel, saying, "Two males. 19.

Now, furthermore, having purchased a banyan shoot that bears fruit on both sides, is unscarred, and is not infested by worms, for twenty-one barley grains or beans, he should cause it to rise up, saying, "O all plants, being well-disposed, bestow your vigor upon this [shoot], for she will perform this rite.
20. Having brought it, he should place it in the air. 21.
A young girl, a celibate student, or a Brahmin woman who has taken vows should grind [the substances] without receiving anything in return.
Having bathed her and laid her down, he should pour [the mixture] into her right nostril with the mantra, "The man is Agni.
Then, in her fourth or sixth month, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) is performed for her.

Having bathed her and clothed her in an unwashed garment, the husband, having offered oblations, should stand behind her and once part the hair-parting with a branch of a fruit-bearing tree and with a porcupine quill that has three white spots, reciting: "This tree is full of sap... (RV 10.97.11).
There is a *sthālīpāka* of rice and peas (*kṛsara*).
He should ask her, as she gazes at the clarified butter placed to the north: "What do you see? (25–27).
He should cause [the woman] to recite, "Offspring" (prajā). 28.
When the fetus has become established, the Soṣyantī-homa is performed. 29.
With the two verses beginning, "She who lies across" (yā tiraścī). 30.
One should give him a name beginning with "Asau" (So-and-so);
that [name] is secret.
Before the cutting of the umbilical cord and before the giving of the breast, one should have rice and barley ground by a woman who has not yet given birth.

Taking [the food] with the thumb and the ring finger, he should make the boy eat it with the words, "This is the command" (34), and with ghee using the mantra, "May wisdom [come to you]" (35). Thus ends the second section.

On the third day after birth, at dawn on the third lunar day, having bathed the boy when the moon has set and the quarters are calm, the father, with palms joined in reverence, should worship the moon. Having covered [the child] with a clean cloth, the mother should hand him over with his head toward the north. Having gone behind the back [of the child], she should stand to the north.

Having worshipped with the three verses beginning "O thou of fair boundaries," and having handed him over to his mother facing northward, he should pour out a handful of water with the verse "Whatever here. He does this twice silently.
After birth, one should give him a name after ten nights, a hundred nights, a year, or a full year.

Having bathed the boy and seated him while he is covered with a clean cloth, the mother should hand him over with his head toward the north. (7) Having gone behind him, she should sit down to the north.
(8) Having offered oblations, she should touch his principal vital breaths with the mantra "Who art thou? (9)
One should give him a name, beginning with "This one," and having first addressed the mother [by that name] at the end of the mantra.
Having returned from a journey, he should take hold of his son's head with the verse, "From limb by limb... (RV 10.85.46).
He should kiss him with the formula, "Of cattle thee... (RV 10.85.47).
For a daughter, he should do so silently.
In the third year, the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) takes place;

at that time, to the south are placed the barber, hot water, a mirror, a razor, and a bunch of *piñjūlī* grass made of *udumbara* wood (16–17). To the north are placed cow-dung from a bull, *kṛsara* porridge, and a vessel of cooked food prepared for no sacred purpose (18).
The mother, having taken the boy, should look at the barber while meditating on Agni, thinking, "Having offered [the oblation], he has come here";
she should look at the hot water while meditating on Vāyu, thinking, "With heat... (uṣṇena).
With "The waters," he moistens [the hair] (22).
With "Of Viṣṇu," he looks into a mirror or one made of udumbara wood (23).
With "O herb," having placed seven darbha-grass tufts with their tips pointing upwards (24).
With the blade of a mirror or one made of udumbara wood, saying "svadhite," he should draw it forward three times toward the east on the right side with [the mantra] "yena pūṣā.
Having cut it once with a metal blade, he should place the hair on a bull's dung cake.
In this same manner, [he should perform the rite] toward the north after [the west].

(28) Having grasped his son’s head, he should mutter the *tryāyuṣa* [mantra]. (29) Having moved toward the north, he should have [the child] made auspicious according to the custom of his lineage and family. (30)
They should bury the hair in the forest; some place it in a clump of grass;
a cow is the sacrificial fee.
Thus ends the third section.
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in his eighth year;
the time for this does not expire until the sixteenth year.
In the eleventh [month], a Kṣatriya;
for him, after the twenty-second [day]; in the twelfth [month], a Vaiśya.

Having covered it with a large, well-washed, and decorated cloth from the twenty-fourth [verse], and having offered an oblation into the fire with the mantra "O Lord of Vows," he should cause the boy to stand to the north of the fire facing west and make him join his palms in añjali.
And he himself should perform [the sprinkling] from above.
Standing to the south, the mantra-knowing Brāhmaṇa should fill his joined palms with water for the teacher. While the teacher is looking on, he should mutter the mantra: "O guest! (āgantra).
When asked, "What is your name?", he should state his name for salutation based on either a deity or a lunar mansion, saying, "I am so-and-so.
Having poured out water, the teacher should take hold of his joined palms with his own right and left hands, reciting the mantra "Of the god...
He should then turn him clockwise while reciting "Of the sun... (Sūryasya).
Having touched his right shoulder, he should touch the uncovered navel with the words, "Of the vital breaths... (15).
Then he should entrust him with the verses beginning with "End-maker" (16).
[He should place] the right shoulder [of the garment] with the words, "For Prajāpati, thee! (17).
With his left hand [he takes] the left [hand of the student] with the formula, "For the sake of the god...

(18). Having given the command, "You are a student of sacred knowledge" (19), and having sat down, while binding the girdle of *muñja* grass around him who has bent his right knee and joined his palms in reverence, he should cause him to recite: "This [girdle] from ill-spoken words... (20).

"Recite, sir!"—with these words he should approach [the teacher]. Then the teacher recites for him the Sāvitrī verse, foot by foot, hemistich by hemistich, and then the whole; thus he should cause him to recite the Sāvitrī.
He should also cause him to recite the Mahāvyāhṛtis one by one.
And he gives him the syllable *oṃ* (24), a staff of wood (25),
[and makes him say] "O you of good fame, make me of good fame" (26).
He should place a fuel-stick on the fire with the words, "A fuel-stick for Agni.
He should go about begging alms,
beginning first with his mother.
Then other friends [should] offer alms to the teacher;
he should remain silent until sunset.
For three nights, one should avoid alkaline substances, salt, and milk.
Thus ends the fourth section.
Regarding the Godāna rite, the procedure is like that of the Cūḍākaraṇa. 1.
One should have the hair and beard shaved together.
Cows, horses, and sheep— pairs of each distinct species— are the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā),
or alternatively, a cow for all of them.
The goat [is for] the receiving of the hair; 5.
the initiation has been described; 6.
[he shall not eat] for a year [if he intends] not to practice [the vow]; 7.
8. Unappointed [sex], 9. likewise [sex] with ornaments, 10.
[sex] while lying on a lower level.
He should not eat honey or meat.
He should avoid sexual intercourse, shaving, bathing, rubbing [the body], cleaning the teeth, and washing the feet.
His semen must not be emitted through desire.
He shall not mount a vehicle yoked with oxen (14); nor shall he wear shoes in the village (15).
Wearing a girdle, wandering for alms, carrying a staff, offering fuel-sticks, performing ritual ablutions, and morning salutation are his constant duties (16).
The Godāna, Vrātika, Ādityavrata, Upaniṣad, and Jyeṣṭhasāmika vows last for one year each. According to some, the Ādityavrata does not exist; those who perform it wear only a single garment.
The sun does not set [during this rite],
nor do the waters overflow;
there are twelve, nine, six, or three verses of the Śakvarī meters as optional alternatives.
Wearing black garments (23),
eating black food (24),
and remaining dependent upon the teacher (25).
He should stand during the day (26) and sit during the night (27);
according to some, for one year, provided he has heard [the Veda] from his predecessors (28).
To one who has fasted and whose eyes are bound, he should cause [the verses] to be recited:
"So that it may not consume me. In the morning, they look toward those things which they think will not consume them—water, fire, the calf, and the sun.

"I have looked upon the waters," [he says]; "I have looked upon the light," [he says regarding] fire; "I have looked upon the cattle," [he says regarding] the calf; "I have looked upon the radiant one," [he says regarding] the sun; then he should release his speech.
A cow is the sacrificial fee (32);
or a bronze vessel, a garment, and gold (33).
At the Anupravacanīya rites, one should offer clarified butter with the verses "Ṛcam," "Sāmam," and "Sadasaspatim" (34).

In the event of touching a city-pillar, being addressed harshly behind one's back, or the twitching of an eye; or if one has risen while the sun is still up, or has gone to sleep while the sun is still out, or has been touched by anything impure by the senses—one should offer an oblation with the two verses beginning "punarmām" (VS 12.40–41).
Or one may offer two fuel-sticks smeared with clarified butter.
Or, in the case of minor offenses, one should simply recite [the relevant mantra]. In the case of minor offenses, one should simply recite.
Thus ends the fifth section;
thus ends the second chapter.
At the time of the ritual bath, he sits surrounded in front of the teacher's family. 1.
The teacher faces north; [the fire] has its tips directed eastward—thus for one desiring spiritual luster;
in a cow-pen for one desiring cattle.
One who desires fame in the assembly should cause water to ferment with all medicinal herbs (sarvauṣadha) and with fragrant substances (surabhi).
The teacher should sprinkle him with those waters, both cold and warm, or he himself may do so by means of the mantra-salutation;
some say that both should do so. Then the teacher should say: "With this [mantra], this one... (tenemam).
He should pour out a handful of water with the verse "ye apsu" (11),
with the verse "yad apām" (12),
and silently (13).
With the mantra "yo rocanaḥ," he should sprinkle himself; with the mantra "yena striyam," and silently as well. 14–16.

One should worship the rising sun with the [hymn] beginning "The rising one" (udyann), or one should combine [the verses]; while spreading them out, one should collect them together with [the formula] "Thou art the eye. (17–19)
With the verse "uduttamam," he should loosen his girdle (20).
Having consumed [the sacrificial food], he should have his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, except for the top-knot (21).
Adorned and wearing new clothes, he should put on a garland with the verse "śrīḥ" (22).
With the words, "You two are leaders," he takes up the two sandals;
with the words, "You are a Gandharva," he should take up a bamboo staff.
Having approached the teacher, he should look upon the assembly as if it were a Yakṣa.
With the mantra, "The lips are the cover," he should touch the principal vital breaths (26).
He should touch the chariot yoked with oxen with the mantra, "O Lord of the Forest" (27).
With the mantra, "Thou art the rider," he should mount it (28).
Having set out toward the east or the north, he should turn to the right. Some say that when he has returned, an *arghya* offering should be presented.
From this point forward, he should be of mature character.
One should not desire to joke with one who has not yet grown pubic hair (32),
nor with one who is naked (33), nor with a woman in her menses (34).

35. One should not eat food prepared by a female ascetic of the same lineage. 36. One should not eat food that has been twice-cooked or has been kept overnight, except for vegetables, meat, and preparations of barley flour. 37.

One should not perform the gathering of fruits, looking into a well, running during rain, or personally carrying sandals; nor should one wear a garland that lacks fragrance, unless it is a golden garland.
One should not utter "Bhadra" in vain (41). One desiring prosperity should drive the cows away with the words "Imāḥ" (42). When they have returned, [he should address them] as "Madhumatīḥ" (43).

One desiring prosperity should lick the forehead of the first-born calf before the mother licks it and swallow [the saliva], thinking, "Of cows. (44) When cows have recently calved, one should offer a libation of melted butter at night in the cow-pen with the verse beginning, "By means of gathering.
(45) Furthermore, one should mark the ears of a pair of calves with the word, "The world" (*bhuvanam*). (46)
Before the man [is born],
he should consecrate the blood with the mantra "Not so" (na iti).
He should consecrate the extended cord with the mantra "This is the cord" (iyaṃ tantī).
Thus ends the first section.
On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, having brought forward the domestic fire, one should smear the ground in each direction at a distance of one additional step.

Having placed barley-meal (saktu) taken in a single scoop onto the ladle and poured water onto the previously smeared spot, one should offer the oblation (bali) with the mantra, "He who [dwells] in the east... (Yaḥ prācyām). 2.
He should pour out the remainder of the water;
having touched water, he should do so toward each direction according to its respective characteristic mark.
Between the south-west and [the fire], there is the path for movement around the fire.

Having poured the remnants from the winnowing basket into the fire, and having gone half-way between the *atipraṇītā* and the *anatipraṇītā*, he should place his hands palm-downward and mutter: "Homage to the Earth! (6).

Then, having stood up and worshipped the bunch of *darbha* grass with the verse, "Soma is King" (7), he should take unbroken grains (*akṣata*), go out of the village toward the east or the north, and offer them with his joined palms using the four verses beginning, "O Rākā! (8).
Having first stepped forward, he should mutter "O Vasuvan, prosper! three times for each cardinal direction and three times for each intermediate direction.
Looking upward, he should offer it to the divine hosts;
looking sideways, to the other (human) hosts.
Looking downwards and returning [to the fire], he should eat the unhusked grains (akṣata) without looking at them.

On the following day, having prepared flour of unhusked grains and placed it in a new vessel, he should offer the bali-oblations after sunset until the Āgrahāyaṇī festival. On the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, they should perform the formal recitation of the Vedic texts (upākaraṇa) under the asterism Hasta.
Some say [the ceremony should be performed] on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa;
having offered oblations as at the initiation (*upanayana*),
he should cause [the student] to recite the Sāvitrī.
They should eat King Soma, the parched grains, curd, and the Parvan-offerings with two suitable verses;
on the following day, they should begin teaching it to their disciples.

They should perform the invitatory verses (*anuvākyā*) with the *ṛc* and other [mantras] and with the *prastāva* chants (21). There is a chanting in accordance with the secret texts (*rahasya*) (22), excluding the lightning and thunder (23).
Having studied for four and a half months, the suspension [of study] takes place on the full moon day of Pauṣa (24).
From that time onwards, there is no study during cloudy days (25),
nor during lightning, thunder, or rain (26).
At the conjunction of the three [festivals], at the three junctions of the day (trisaṃdhyam),

on the eighth day, on the new moon, on the full moon of the four-month periods, during the northern course of the sun, and for one night with a "bird's flight" interval (pakṣiṇī rātri) when a fellow student has died.
In the event of a falling meteor, an earthquake, or an eclipse of the luminaries, one should know that these occasions require an *ākālika* [suspension of study].
However, the followers of the Kaṭha and Kauthuma schools maintain that this applies only to the study of the *Kārṣva* [portion of the Veda].
Thus ends the second section.
On the full moon day of Āśvayuja, there is a milk-rice offering (pāyasa) for the Rudras;
one should offer it with the mantra "mā nas toke" (VS 3.18).
One should pour out the curdled milk (payasyā) into the clarified butter (ājya); that is *pṛṣātaka*.
With that [milk], he should sprinkle the cows that have arrived with the mantra, "O Mitra and Varuṇa, let us sprinkle [the cows].
And he should let the calves stay together with their mothers for that night.
At the Navayajña, there is a milk-rice offering (pāyasa) dedicated to Indra and Agni.
One should offer clarified butter with the four verses beginning with "To him who has a hundred weapons" (RV 10.87.1–4),
and subsequently with the verse "May Agni eat it" (RV 10.87.5).
Those who have been initiated should consume the remainder of that [offering].
Having spread [the butter] with water, one should cut off two portions from the new [grain];
three for the Bhṛgus; and [two] portions of water on top.

One should swallow [the food] three times each without chewing it, with the mantra "May it be auspicious for us" (bhadrā naḥ). Or, one may do so with barley using the mantra "Him, that supreme one" (etamu tyam).
One should touch the principal vital breaths with the mantra "Thou art not [to be harmed]" (amosi).
The ritual for Āgrahāyaṇa is explained by [the rules for] Śrāvaṇa (16).
One should not mutter the mantra "Obeisance to Pṛthivī" (17). At nightfall, one should offer oblations of milk-rice with the verse beginning "prathamā" (18).
Having placed his hands downward, he should mutter the verse, "In every domain" (RV 8.45.37).

19. To the west of the fire, having spread a layer of grass with the tips pointing northward on a slope toward the north, the householder sits upon that layer. 20. The others sit in succession behind him. 21.
Immediately thereafter, the wife and the sons [should do so]; 22.
Having placed their hands palms-downward, the householder should mutter the verse beginning with "syonā. 23.
When it has concluded, they should lie down on their right sides, turning toward themselves three times each. 24.
They should perform rites for well-being;
thus it shall be according to the purpose.
After the Āgrahāyaṇī full moon, the three eighth days of the dark fortnights are called Aṣṭakās.
In those [fires], there are eight pot-cooked offerings (sthālīpākas) and eight cakes (apūpas) on the first day;
he should cook them on a potsherd without turning them over.
On the eighth day of the waxing moon, one should offer the Śāka meal as the Anvāhārya; he should sacrifice with the formula, "To Aṣṭakā, svāhā!
Thus ends the third section.
A cow for the middle [deity];
having placed it in front of the fire facing westward, he should sacrifice with the verse, "yat paśavaḥ" (TS 3.1.4.3).
Having sacrificed, he should consecrate it with the mantra, "anu tvā" (TS 3.1.4.3).
He should sprinkle it with as much water as is required, saying, "I sprinkle you, acceptable to the Aṣṭakā.
Having sprinkled it and carried fire around it with a firebrand, he should cause it to drink the sprinkling-water.
Having moved northward, he should cause it to be slaughtered with its head toward the west and its feet toward the north.
When the animal has been consecrated, he should offer the oblation with the verse, "That which the animal... (TS 3.1.4.3).
Its wife should wash its orifices. Having placed two strainers between, he should cut out and extract the omentum.
Having grasped it with two forked branches of a sacrificial tree, one should cook it over the fire.
(10) One should split it when it has become soft.
(11) The rules for the under-layering and the sprinkling of clarified butter are as stated for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. (12)
One should offer the oblation with the formula, "Svāhā to Aṣṭakā. (13) One should extract the portions for the sacrifice from all the limbs. (14) Not from the left thigh. (15)
Having placed the left thigh upon the *kloman*,
he cooks the sacrificial portions and the *sthālīpāka* separately with two different ladles.
Having poured the juice into the bronze vessel (kaṃsa),
and having made the portions (avadāna) on branches of the Plakṣa tree, one should take portions from each [branch] into the bronze vessel.
And from the *sthālīpāka*,
one should offer into the fire either four portions or eight portions;
with two verses each from the [hymn] following the *kaṃsa* verse, one should offer each oblation.
The *sauviṣṭakṛta* offering is on the eighth [day];
"Carry the omentum" (*vaha vapām*) is the omentum-oblation for the ancestors;
"O Jātavedas" (*jātavedaḥ*) is for the deity.
In the case of that which is not known, one follows its instruction; as in the case of the Aṣṭakā,
the sacrificial animal itself is the fee for the animal sacrifice.
A full vessel for the *sthālīpāka*—this is the thirty-first [sūtra].
Thus ends the fourth section.
On the ninth or tenth day, the *anvaṣṭakya* rite is performed. 1.

Having surrounded [the fire] in the south-eastern part, one should churn the fire there in the northern half and bring it forward. (2) One should cook the rice-grains, having taken them once and husked them once, turning to the left and keeping the fire on the right. (3) And [one should take] meat from such-and-such a thigh. (4)
Having carried the oblation toward the south, one should not pour clarified butter over it again.
To the west of the fire, one should dig three trenches to the south, four finger-breadths deep and as wide across at the bottom. One should bring the fire forward from those trenches.

He should strew [grass] (8), and behind the fire he should prepare a sacrificial bed (svastara) by spreading southward-pointed grass so that it slopes toward the south, and upon it he should place a cushion (vṛsī). (10)

From that [meat], he should take a single portion from each; having placed them together in a bronze vessel (*kaṃsa*), he should offer them as a spoonful (*mekṣaṇa-upaghāta*) with the words: "Svāhā to Soma accompanied by the ancestors! Svāhā to Agni, the bearer of the *kavyas*! (12).
With his left hand, he should place a firebrand to the south of the pits, [saying]: "The [obstructors] are driven away" (13).
In the eastern furrow, he should pour water for the father (14);
in the middle furrow, for the grandfather; and in the northern furrow, for the great-grandfather (15).

He should pour the vessels of water into the furrows from right to left, pronouncing the name of each one: "O [Name], wash yourself! And those who follow you here, and those whom you follow—for them and for you, may it be palatable! (16).

In the same manner, having placed the balls of food, he should mutter here: "O ancestors, rejoice; may you be satisfied according to your respective portions. (17) Having spoken thus, he should turn toward the north, drawing in his left arm and turning counter-clockwise.
(18) Having rested and meditating on what is auspicious, while turning back, he should mutter: "The ancestors have rejoiced; they have been satisfied according to their respective portions. (19)

Having rubbed three blades of *darbha* grass into color for the purpose of marking, he should place them in the trenches according to the order of the rice balls; likewise, [he should place] fragrant oil.
From the offering of the rice balls onwards, he should proceed according to the purpose.
Now, the ritual of concealment (nihnavana): 23.
Having placed the hands with palms turned upward on the eastern furrow, [he says] "Homage to you, O fathers, for life; homage to you, O fathers, for vigor. 24.
With the left hand turned upward on the middle furrow, [he says] "Homage to you, O fathers, for the terrible; homage to you, O fathers, for the essence. 25.

With the palms turned upward toward the south, he should offer [oblations] in the western [pit] with the formulas: "Homage to you, O fathers, for the *svadhā* offering; homage to you, O fathers, for your wrath" (26).
Having made the *añjali* gesture, he says "Homage to you" (27).
He should place threads of the sacrificial cord into the pits with the formula: "This is for you" (28), just as he did with the rice balls (*piṇḍa*).
He should consecrate the furrows with the mantra, "Carrying strength" (ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ). 29.
He should cause a woman desiring a son to eat the middle ball of rice with the mantra, "Bestow [seed]" (ādhatta). 30.
He should throw the firebrand into the fire with the mantra, "He has been our messenger" (abhūn no dūtaḥ). 31.
They should carry the vessels back in pairs.
32 This very same is the ritual procedure for the Piṇḍapitṛyajña. 33 One should cook the oblation in the domestic fire (gṛhya-agni). 34
From that very [spot] one should draw the line; there is one furrow;
there is no spreading of grass.
One should offer [the oblation] with the verse, "O Indra, [this is] for the Ekāṣṭakā of the Sthālīpāka. 38.
Thus ends the fifth section;
thus ends the third chapter.

In the case of optional rites (kāmya), one should not eat six meals or three meals; for those rites performed as a constant obligation (nitya), [one should fast] from the beginning; and for those performed on specific occasions (sānnipātika), [one should fast] after [the rite].
Thus, during the performance of sacrifices:
(4) one who observes the half-month vow; (5) if unable [to observe the full vow], one may drink [milk] once a day.
Seated in a forest on grass-blades pointing eastward, he should mutter the *prapada* [section];
thus for one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*),
and as previously stated for one desiring cattle.

One who desires the well-being of cattle should offer oblations of rice and barley while reciting "He who has a thousand arms" (RV 6.47). 10. With whatever he may desire, such as a mango tree, he should give it after consecrating its large fruits with the *kautūhala-mantra*. 11.

Having observed a vow for half a month, on the night of the full moon, having waded waist-deep into a non-flooded lake, he should offer unbroken rice grains from his mouth while reciting the five verses beginning with "Like a tree in the water" (RV 10.73.5–9); this is the ritual pertaining to the earth. 12.
One desiring enjoyment should worship the Sun with the first [verse] while the Lord of Wealth (Arthapati) is looking on;
with the second [verse], one desiring the well-being of large-leaved plants should worship the Sun while he is being served food with unbroken rice grains;
with the third [verse], one desiring the well-being of small animals should worship the Moon with sesame and rice grains.
On the fourth [lunar day], having performed the worship of the Sun, he should rise to attend upon his teacher.
On the fifth, having performed the worship of the Sun, he should go to his home. He should constantly mutter the syllable "Bhūḥ" as a death-warden that cannot be warded off.

At the time of sacrifice, one should offer oblations with the six verses beginning with "From the head over me," with the Vāmadevya *ṛc*s, with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*s), and with the verse addressed to Prajāpati. 19.
This is the "Driving Away of Misfortune" (*alakṣmīnirṇoda*). 20.
On an unsafe path, one should mutter the verse beginning with "Go away from the path. 21.

One who desires glory should worship the sun with the mantra "I am glory," during the forenoon, midday, and afternoon. (22) One should adapt the formula "of the morning" according to the actual time. (23) The worship of the sun with the mantra "The ship of the sun" is a rite for the twilight and a prayer for well-being. (24)
"O you who are rising!"—with these words [he offers] to the east; "O you who are setting!"—with these words to the west.
Thus ends the first section.
One observing the half-month vow should feed Brāhmaṇas at the beginning of the dark fortnight with boiled rice from a bronze vessel.

At other twilights, having smeared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) from the western village, he should offer grains to him with the words "To Bhalāya" and "To Bhallāya. In the same way, at the beginning of the next dark fortnight and so forth,
until the completion of the period of studentship (brahmacarya).
There are one hundred heaps [of earth].

On ground that is reddish-brown, a Brāhmaṇa should choose his dwelling; on red ground, a Kṣatriya; on black ground, a Vaiśya. It should be level, covered with grass, not saline, and not parched; it is a place where water flows toward the west or the north.
In this [place], medicinal plants that are sapless, thorny, or pungent should not exist.
(8) That which is comparable to *darbha* grass brings spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*).
(9) That which has large grasses brings strength (*balya*). (10)

A site suitable for cattle is one with soft grass (11), or where self-formed hollows face in all directions (12). A house with its door facing east brings wealth and fame; one facing north brings sons and cattle; one with doors facing south and west fulfills all desires; and a house-door that faces no particular direction [is neutral] (13).
He should remain secluded; 14.
the oblation is milk; 15. and the cow is black. 16.

Either a goat, or a white one, or even milk-rice; in the middle of the house, he should offer fat or milk-rice mixed with ghee, eight times taken up, with the verse "O Lord of the Dwelling" (Vāstoṣpati),
and those which follow.
Having offered oblations with those [mantras] for the removal of the seven misfortunes (alakṣmī),
he should present the bali-offerings to the directions,
including the intermediate directions, as well as to the upward and downward directions.

In this manner, year after year, or at the two Navayajñas, one who desires that someone come under his control should offer oblations with these two [verses] beginning with "vaśaṃ gamau," while uttering the person's name as "so-and-so"; he will then become subject to his will. Thus ends the second section.
One who observes the vow for half a month, desiring the continuity of his lineage, should offer a hundred stakes made of iron with the *ekākṣarī* mantra on the night of the full moon.
One desiring long life should offer stakes made of *khadira* wood.

Now, another [rite]: having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, having leveled a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), or having heated it with wild cow-dung on a mountain, and having removed the embers, one should offer oblations with the mouth.
Twelve villages [are gained] when it blazes;
at least three when there is smoke. One should offer *kambūka* fruits every morning and evening; one's livelihood shall not diminish.
One should offer the *paṇya-homa* with the mantra "idam aham imam" (7);
one should offer the *pūrṇa-homa* on the day of sacrifice (8); one who desires companions should offer [the oblation] with the mantra "indrāgnī avadāt" (9).

Having fasted for eight nights, facing either east or north at a crossroads outside the village, he should kindle a fire with fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood; using a *sruva*-ladle and a *camasa*-cup, he should offer oblations with the words "Food indeed! and "Prosperity indeed! (10).
[The offering] in the village is with the third [formula]: "Of food indeed! (11).
He attains lordship (12).
One should offer milk-rice (*pāyasa*) into the fire in a cow-pen for those who are suffering from illness (13).
On an unsafe road, one should tie knots in the hems of the garments of one's companions and perform rites for their well-being (14).
One who desires to obtain a thousand measures of food should offer a thousand oblations with these two [mantras], beginning with "To hunger, svāhā" (15).
One desiring cattle [should offer] with the dung of a pair of calves; one desiring small cattle [should offer] with the dung of a pair of sheep. 16.
One should offer in the evening and in the morning with green cow-dung; his livelihood shall not diminish.
17. Thus ends the third section.

Sprinkling water over one bitten by something poisonous, he should mutter: "Do not fear. (1) A Snātaka, entering [his home], should set down a bamboo staff as a protection for his horse, saying: "May there be well-being. (2) Saying:
"It is slain," he should sprinkle water over a place infested with worms while muttering [the appropriate mantra]. (3)
If it concerns cattle, one should fetch a clod of earth from a furrow in the afternoon; in the morning, while scattering dust over it, one should mutter [the verse].
(4) When about to accept the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), one should mutter, while stepping forward, "This I [place] upon this. (5) Or [one may do so] when they are honoring him. (6)
They announce each of the following three times: the seat, water for the feet, the guest-offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamanīya), and the honey-mixture (madhuparka), as well as the cow.
Having spread the seat toward the north, he should sit upon it with the verse, "The plants which... (RV 10.97.1).

If there are two [verses], he should look at the waters with the second verse beginning "apaḥ paśyet" (he should look at the waters) and "yato devīḥ" (from whence the goddesses). He should sprinkle his left foot with the verse beginning "savyam" (the left).
"The right one, the right one," [he says] thirteen times;
both [feet] with the remainder [of the verse].
"Thou art the protector of the kingdom of food," [with these words] he should accept the water for honoring (arghya). 15.
"Thou art glory," [with these words] he offers water for sipping (ācamanīya).
(16) "Thou art the glory of glory," [with these words] he offers the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
(17) He should drink it three times [with the formula]: "Of glory, of greatness, of fortune. (18)
The fourth [act] is performed silently. (19) One should give the remnants of the meal to a Brāhmaṇa who is not a relative.
(20) One should address the cow that has been recognized with the mantra, "Release the cow," and should utter the name of the person being honored, saying, "and of so-and-so. (21)
Thus, in a non-sacrificial rite, [one says] "do it"; in a sacrificial rite, [one says] "perform it.
A teacher, an officiating priest, a bath-graduate, a king, one with whom one has a marriage alliance, and a friend—these six are worthy of the *arghya* offering.
One should not invite those who have been excluded from the annual Śrāddha;
and [one should not invite them] at a second sacrifice or a second marriage—
this is the fourth section.
Thus ends the fourth chapter;
the Khādira Gṛhyasūtra is completed.
